title: Counting what is left
objectives: Find the chance of a second draw by counting what the first draw left
Multiply along a branch to find the chance of two draws together
See why an unseen first draw does not change the second

screens.title: Counting what is left
screens.prose: Draw from a bag without putting anything back, and the bag changes under you. Each draw has to be counted on what the last one left.
A bag holds 3 red counters and 2 blue ones. You draw one, look at it, and keep it out. It is red.
screens.question: What is the chance the next counter is red too?

options.why: You put the red counter back. It stays out, so 4 counters are left and 2 of them are red.
You took a red out of the reds but kept 5 counters in the bag. One fewer counter is left.
You took a counter out of the total but not out of the reds. The one you drew was red.

hints.text: How many counters are in the bag after the first draw?
The red branch is the draw that happened.
4 counters are left: 2 red and 2 blue. So the chance of red is 2 out of 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the counters that are left in the bag, and the reds among them.

explain.text: You took one red out, which leaves 2 red and 2 blue. The second draw is counted on those 4 counters. So the chance is $\tfrac{2}{4}$, down from $\tfrac{3}{5}$.

screens.prose: Name the counters R1, R2, R3, B1 and B2. Each cell is one ordered pair of draws. The grey diagonal is impossible: a counter cannot come out twice.
screens.question: Shade every pair of draws where both counters are red.

hints.text: Which rows start with a red counter? Which columns end with one?
Both-red pairs sit in the top-left block of rows R1 to R3 and columns R1 to R3.

feedback.correct: Six ordered pairs are both red.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shade only pairs where both counters are red, and skip the diagonal.

byKey.with-diagonal: You shaded the diagonal. A counter cannot be drawn twice, so those cells never happen.
byKey.r1c4: R1 then B1 ends with a blue counter.
byKey.r4c1: B1 then R1 starts with a blue counter.
byKey.r2c5: R2 then B2 ends with a blue counter.

explain.text: You shaded the six pairs such as R1 R2 and R2 R1, all in the top-left block. The diagonal stays empty because no counter is drawn twice. In all, the bag has 20 possible ordered pairs.

screens.prose: Knowing the first counter is red keeps rows R1 to R3: 12 cells. We write $P(\text{2nd red} \mid \text{1st red})$ for the chance of a red second draw **given** a red first.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{2nd red} \mid \text{1st red})$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance the second is red given the first is red

hints.text: How many cells are left in rows R1 to R3?
The outlined rows are the draws with a red first counter.
12 cells are left, and 6 of them are shaded both red. 6 out of 12 is $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

feedback.correct: 6 both-red cells among the 12 with a red first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count inside the outlined rows only.

byKey.all-cells: You divided by all 20 cells. The news keeps only the 12 cells with a red first.
byKey.put-back: That is $\tfrac{3}{5}$, the chance with the first counter put back. It stays out.

explain.text: You counted 6 shaded cells inside the 12 with a red first counter. That matches the bag: 2 reds among 4 counters. The grid and the bag agree, $\tfrac{6}{12} = \tfrac{2}{4}$.

screens.prose: Back to the tree. Suppose the first counter had been blue instead.
screens.question: After a blue first draw, what is the chance the second is red? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of red after a blue first draw

hints.text: Which counters are left after a blue one comes out?
Follow the blue branch to its second draw.
4 counters are left: all 3 reds and 1 blue. So the chance of red is 3 out of 4.

feedback.correct: All 3 reds are still in a bag of 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count what is left after a blue counter comes out.

byKey.put-back: You put the blue counter back. It stays out, so only 4 counters are left.
byKey.after-red: That is the chance after a red first draw. A blue came out here, so all 3 reds remain.
byKey.blue: That is the chance the second is blue. The question asks for red.

explain.text: You followed the blue branch: 3 reds and 1 blue are left. So the second draw is red with chance $\tfrac{3}{4}$. The same question gets a different answer on each branch, because each branch leaves a different bag.

screens.prose: Now no news at all. Before you draw anything, ask about both draws together.
screens.question: What is the chance both counters are red? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: On the grid, how many cells were both red, out of how many?
The path red then red runs along the top of the tree.
The grid has 6 both-red cells out of 20. On the tree that is $\tfrac{3}{5}$ of the time, then $\tfrac{2}{4}$ of that.

feedback.correct: 6 of the 20 ordered pairs are both red.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count both-red pairs out of all 20, or follow the top path of the tree.

byKey.put-back: That is $\tfrac{3}{5} \times \tfrac{3}{5}$, as if the first counter went back. It stays out.
byKey.given: That is the second draw given the first was red. Both red also needs the first to be red.
byKey.first-only: That is the first draw alone. The second counter must be red too.

explain.text: You found 6 both-red pairs among 20, which is 0.3. Along the tree, a red first happens $\tfrac{3}{5}$ of the time, and then a red second $\tfrac{2}{4}$ of that. So $\tfrac{3}{5} \times \tfrac{2}{4} = \tfrac{6}{20}$ gives the same answer.

screens.prose: Same bag, no news. Someone draws the first counter and hides it in their pocket without looking.
screens.question: What is the chance the second counter is red? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance the second counter is red

hints.text: Which cells have a red second counter? Look down the columns.
Columns R1 to R3 hold every pair that ends in red.
Each of the three red columns has 4 cells, so 12 of the 20 pairs end in red.

feedback.correct: 12 of the 20 pairs end in red, the same $\tfrac{3}{5}$ as the first draw.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells in the red columns, out of all 20.

byKey.assumed-red: You assumed the first counter was red. Nobody saw it, so both branches are still possible.
byKey.average: You averaged $\tfrac{2}{4}$ and $\tfrac{3}{4}$ equally. A red first is more likely than a blue one, so weight it more.
byKey.assumed-blue: You assumed the first counter was blue. Nobody saw it, so both branches are still possible.

explain.text: You counted the red columns: 12 of the 20 pairs end in red, so the chance is $\tfrac{3}{5}$. A hidden first draw tells you nothing, so the second draw looks just like the first. The bag only changes for you once you see what came out.

screens.prose: To get both red, you took the chance of the first draw, then the chance of the second on what was left: $$P(A \cap B) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)$$ Each factor is counted on the bag as it stands at that draw.
screens.question: Which product gives the chance of blue, then blue?

options.why: You put the first blue counter back. It stays out, so the second draw is from 4 counters with 1 blue.
You took a counter out of the total but kept both blues. The one that came out was blue.
That is the second draw given the first was blue. You also need the chance the first was blue.

hints.text: What is the chance the first counter is blue? What is left after it?
The first is blue with chance $\tfrac{2}{5}$. That leaves 1 blue among 4, so multiply by $\tfrac{1}{4}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the first draw's chance, then the second's on what is left.

explain.text: You took $\tfrac{2}{5}$ for a blue first, then $\tfrac{1}{4}$ for a blue from the 4 left. Multiplying along the branch gives $\tfrac{1}{10}$, which matches the 2 blue-blue cells of the 20.

screens.prose: Why does multiplying work? Counting gave $P(\text{both red}) = \tfrac{6}{20}$. Split that fraction through the 12 cells with a red first: $$\frac{6}{20} = \frac{12}{20} \times \;?$$
screens.question: What fraction completes the line?

hints.text: What do you multiply $\tfrac{12}{20}$ by to get $\tfrac{6}{20}$?
The missing factor counts both-red cells inside the 12 with a red first.
$\tfrac{12}{20} \times \tfrac{6}{12} = \tfrac{6}{20}$, because the 12s cancel. And $\tfrac{6}{12}$ is $P(\text{2nd red} \mid \text{1st red})$.

feedback.correct: The 12s cancel, and $\tfrac{6}{12}$ is the chance of a red second given a red first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the factor that turns $\tfrac{12}{20}$ into $\tfrac{6}{20}$.

byKey.put-back: $\tfrac{3}{5}$ is the chance of red with the first counter put back. Inside the 12 red-first cells, 6 are both red.
byKey.upside-down: That factor is upside down. It would make the product bigger than $\tfrac{12}{20}$.
byKey.whole: That repeats the left side. You need the factor that takes $\tfrac{12}{20}$ down to $\tfrac{6}{20}$.

explain.text: You found $\tfrac{6}{12}$: multiplying by it cancels the 12s. The first factor is $P(\text{1st red})$ and the second is $P(\text{2nd red} \mid \text{1st red})$. So the product rule is the count, split into two steps.

screens.prose: A portfolio holds 10 stocks, and 4 of them beat the market last year. An analyst reviews two different stocks picked at random.
screens.question: What is the chance both picks beat the market? Give a decimal or a fraction.

widget.label: Chance both picks beat the market
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{12}{90} = \tfrac{2}{15}$, or about 0.133.

hints.text: What is the chance the first pick beat the market? What is left after it?
Follow the top path: beats, then beats.
The first beats with chance $\tfrac{4}{10}$. Then 3 winners are left among 9, so multiply by $\tfrac{3}{9}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the first pick's chance by the second's, counted on the 9 stocks left.

byKey.put-back: That is $\tfrac{4}{10} \times \tfrac{4}{10}$, as if the same stock could be picked twice. The second pick comes from 9.
byKey.second-only: That is the second pick given the first beat. Multiply by the chance the first beat.
byKey.first-only: That is the first pick alone. Both picks have to beat the market.

explain.text: You multiplied along the top branch: $\tfrac{4}{10}$, then $\tfrac{3}{9}$ from the 9 stocks left. That gives $\tfrac{12}{90} \approx 0.133$. Sampling without repeats is drawing without replacement, the same bag in a new setting.

ideas: Drawing without replacement changes what is left for the next draw.
The chance of both is the first chance times the second, counted on what is left.
With no news about the first draw, the second draw has the same chance as the first.

formula.name: Multiplication rule
formula.note: Read along a branch: each chance is counted on what the earlier draws left.

summary.trap: A first draw you did not see does not change the second. Only news about it does.

quiz.prose: A box holds 4 good chips and 2 faulty ones. Two chips are taken out, one after the other, without replacement.
quiz.question: The first chip is faulty. What is the chance the second is faulty too?

options.why: You put the first faulty chip back. It stays out, so 5 chips are left with 1 faulty.
You took a chip out of the total but not out of the faulty ones. The one that came out was faulty.
That is the chance both are faulty. The first chip is already known to be faulty.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count what is left in the box after a faulty chip comes out.

explain.text: Taking out a faulty chip leaves 5 chips, 1 of them faulty. So the chance is $\tfrac{1}{5}$.

quiz.prose: Two cards are dealt from a standard 52-card deck, without replacement.
quiz.question: What is the chance both are aces? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the first ace's chance by the second's, counted on the 51 cards left.

byKey.put-back: That is $\tfrac{4}{52} \times \tfrac{4}{52}$, as if the first ace went back. It stays out.
byKey.second-only: That is the second ace given the first. Multiply by the chance the first is an ace.

explain.text: The first card is an ace with chance $\tfrac{4}{52}$. That leaves 3 aces among 51 cards. So both are aces with chance $\tfrac{4}{52} \times \tfrac{3}{51} = \tfrac{1}{221}$.

quiz.prose: The bag holds 3 red and 2 blue counters again. The first counter is drawn and put aside unseen.
quiz.question: What is the chance the second counter is blue?

options.why: You assumed the first counter was blue. Nobody saw it.
You assumed the first counter was red. Nobody saw it.
That is red then blue. Blue then blue also ends in blue, so add $\tfrac{1}{10}$.

feedback.correct: Unseen, the first draw changes nothing: $\tfrac{2}{5}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up every path that ends in blue.

explain.text: Two paths end in blue: red then blue, $\tfrac{3}{10}$, and blue then blue, $\tfrac{1}{10}$. Together they make $\tfrac{4}{10} = \tfrac{2}{5}$, the same as the first draw.
